seoTitle: eBay Refund Guide: Get Your Money Back
metaDescription: Learn how to request a refund on eBay when an item didn't arrive, was damaged, or wasn't as described, and how to escalate an unresolved case.
intro: If an eBay order arrives damaged, doesn't match the listing photos, or never shows up at all, buyer protection is there to get your money back — but the process only works smoothly if you document the problem clearly and go through the right channel first. This guide covers checking a seller before you rely on them, opening a direct conversation about the issue, and writing the kind of message that gets a refund approved instead of ignored.

steps.heading: Check the seller's feedback before you rely on their word
steps.body: Every eBay listing has an "About this seller" panel showing their feedback percentage, how many items they've sold, and how long they've been on the platform, plus a running feed of recent reviews filtered by rating category — value, satisfaction, condition, fit, appearance, and quality. Before you escalate anything, skim this feedback for patterns: a seller with thousands of sales and a stray complaint about slow shipping is a different situation than one with recent, repeated complaints about items not matching photos. This context matters once you're writing your refund request, since referencing a seller's own feedback history can strengthen your case if the problem you're having matches what others have already reported.

image.caption: A listing's seller panel and feedback feed, showing ratings broken out by value, satisfaction, condition, fit, appearance, and quality.

steps.heading: Open a direct conversation with the seller
steps.body: From the item or your Purchase History, use the Contact option to open eBay's built-in messaging panel, which keeps the conversation attached to that specific order and item. Message threads opened this way are timestamped and tied to the transaction, which is exactly the paper trail buyer protection cases rely on — it's a meaningfully stronger position than emailing a seller directly or messaging them on a third-party app. eBay also actively screens these threads for anyone trying to move a deal off-platform, so keep the conversation here rather than agreeing to settle things outside eBay's system.

image.caption: The messaging panel opened directly from a purchased item, ready to send a message tied to that specific order.

steps.heading: Describe the problem clearly and attach proof
steps.body: Write exactly what's wrong in plain terms — for a damaged or misrepresented item, something like "the item is damaged, the colors are different than the original in the pic you showed" gives the seller (and eBay, if it escalates) an unambiguous statement of the issue rather than a vague complaint. Attach photos using the image icon next to the message box; a clear picture of the damage or the color mismatch next to the listing photo does more to resolve a case than paragraphs of explanation. There's also a checkbox to send a copy of the message to your own email, which is worth ticking so you have your own record outside eBay in case you need it later.

image.caption: A message describing item damage and a color mismatch, written in the seller's chat thread with the option to email yourself a copy.

steps.heading: Start the formal return or refund request
steps.body: If the seller doesn't respond helpfully within a reasonable window, go to Purchase History, select the order, and open the formal request — Return this item for something that doesn't match the listing or is damaged, or Item not received if it simply never showed up. This starts an official case with its own tracking and deadlines, separate from the informal message thread, and it's the step that actually puts eBay's buyer protection guarantee behind your claim rather than just a seller's goodwill.

steps.heading: Escalate if the seller denies or ignores the request
steps.body: Sellers have a set window to respond to a formal request, and if they deny it without a reasonable explanation or simply let it sit, you can ask eBay to step in and review the case directly. Having the earlier message thread with your clear description and photos attached makes this review faster, since eBay's team can see exactly what was reported and when, rather than having to piece the timeline together from scratch.

steps.heading: Track the refund once it's approved
steps.body: An approved refund typically shows up back on your original payment method within a matter of days, whether that's a card, PayPal balance, or bank account depending on how you paid. Check that account rather than only your eBay case status, since the case itself will often show as "resolved" before the money has actually posted. If it hasn't landed after the timeframe eBay quotes you, that message thread and case number are what you'll reference to follow up.

faq.question: What if my eBay item never arrived?
faq.answer: Open a formal Item Not Received request from your Purchase History. It's worth messaging the seller first to see if they can explain the delay, but the formal request is what puts buyer protection behind your claim.

faq.question: What if the seller denies my refund request?
faq.answer: If the seller denies or ignores your request within the allowed window, you can ask eBay to step in and review the case directly, using your message thread and any photos as evidence.

faq.question: Do I need photos to request a refund?
faq.answer: Photos make a real difference, especially for damaged, fake, or not-as-described items. Attach them directly in the message thread alongside a clear written description of the problem.

faq.question: Should I check seller feedback before buying?
faq.answer: Yes — the About this seller panel on every listing shows their feedback percentage and recent reviews by category, which can flag a pattern of issues before you ever place an order.

faq.question: How can I check if my refund was processed?
faq.answer: Check the account tied to your original payment method — card, PayPal, or bank — rather than relying only on the case status, since eBay sometimes marks a case resolved before the funds have posted.
